contentBlocks.text: Before we travel to ancient Mesopotamia and Egypt, we need a real framework: what actually makes a group of people a 'civilization,' rather than just a village or a camp?

Historians generally look for several characteristics together: cities (large, permanent settlements), organized government (leaders and laws), specialized jobs (not everyone farms — some make tools, others govern, others create art), social classes (different levels of status and wealth), religion (shared beliefs and practices), a writing or record-keeping system, and advanced technology or art. A small farming village might have some of these, but a true civilization has most or all of them working together. Think of your own community: which of these seven characteristics does it have?
You now have a real framework for identifying a civilization. Tomorrow we'll discover why almost every early civilization formed in one specific kind of place: next to a major river.

objectives: List the seven characteristics historians use to identify a civilization
Apply this framework to their own community as a check for understanding
teacherGuide.facilitationScript:
1. Ask the child what they already think 'civilization' means.
2. Introduce the seven characteristics one at a time with concrete examples.
3. Apply the framework to the child's own community together.
4. Complete the worksheet.
5. Preview tomorrow's topic: why rivers mattered so much to early civilizations.
differentiationTips: Struggling: focus on just 4 of the 7 characteristics (cities, government, jobs, writing) as the core set
Ready for more: ask them to think of a group that has SOME but not all 7 characteristics, and discuss whether it counts as a civilization
This framework will be used repeatedly across the whole world-history course, worth taking real time to make it stick
teacherGuide.answerKey: 1. The seven characteristics are cities, government, specialized jobs, social classes, religion, writing, and advanced technology/art. 2. Answers will vary for the child's own community analysis.
teacherGuide.standardsRationale: Establishes the C3 Framework History dimension's foundational analytical framework (what defines a civilization) before surveying specific civilizations, matching the course's own 'ancient civilizations' description.
